title: Human Security

cards.h: From state security to people's security
cards.b:
For decades 'security' meant defending borders. Human security turns the question around: secure from what, and whom? Hunger, disease, violence at home, repression and climate shocks kill more people than wars. It links Paper II's global concerns with development and rights.

Expect this as a 10 or 15 mark question, or as a supporting example inside a longer answer. Read the cards in order, then test yourself with the quiz.
It grew from Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen's human development work and the end of the Cold War 'peace dividend'.

1. Economic: assured income, jobs.
  2. Food: access to enough food.
  3. Health: freedom from disease.
  4. Environmental: clean air, water, climate stability.
  5. Personal: safety from violence, crime, abuse.
  6. Community: cultural identity, protection from ethnic violence.
  7. Political: civil and political rights.

Co-chaired by Sadako Ogata and Amartya Sen, its report Human Security Now (2003) defined the aim as protecting the 'vital core' of all lives, through protection (top-down: states and institutions) and empowerment (bottom-up: people's capabilities). It links to Sen's capability approach.

Canada (Lloyd Axworthy) pursued 'freedom from fear': the Ottawa landmines treaty (1997), the ICC (1998), child soldiers. Japan stressed 'freedom from want', with the UN Trust Fund for Human Security (1999). The R2P doctrine (ICISS 2001; adopted at the 2005 World Summit) covers genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity. UNGA resolution 66/290 (2012) set a common understanding.

Recent crises test the concept. Pandemics (COVID-19, 2020-22) showed health as a security matter. Climate change displaces millions and strains food and water. Cyber threats, forced migration and refugees, and conflict-linked hunger add pressure. Human security thinking says the response must combine early warning, social protection and local participation, and not rely on force alone. Note that threats are interlinked: drought raises food prices, which feed unrest.

• Too broad: Roland Paris (2001) called it a vague, 'hot air' concept that cannot guide policy.
  • Securitisation: calling poverty a security issue can justify military or intrusive action.
  • Intervention: used by powerful states selectively (Libya 2011, Iraq 2003).
  • State vs people: states can be the main threat, but they also deliver protection.
  • Realists: security remains about states and force.

Compare: Human development (growth of capabilities), human rights (legal claims), R2P (a narrower, force-linked doctrine), feminist security (everyday safety), Sustainable Development Goals (2015). Human security adds downside risk and vulnerability to development thinking.

India accepts people-centred development but is wary of the language of intervention and R2P, stressing sovereignty. Domestic expressions: MGNREGA (2005), National Food Security Act (2013), Right to Education (2009), Ayushman Bharat, disaster management, and Maoist and insurgency-affected area policies. India's COVID vaccine diplomacy (Vaccine Maitri, 2021) is a human-security story at the international level.
